# Abstract

Between the Carolingian frontier wars of 800AD and the arrival of *Yersinia pestis* at Constantinople in 1347AD, the belt of territories stretching from the Baltic coast to the Aegean underwent one of the sharpest demographic transformations in European history. Across 1.499.589,5 km² divided into eight analytical sub-regions — the Piast Kingdom of Poland, Bohemia and Moravia, the Kingdom of Hungary and Slovakia, Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania, the Baltic Lands, Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia, Mediaeval Serbia, Montenegro and Albania and the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece — MAGNETIC reconstructs a combined population rising from 8,39M in 800AD (5,59 inhabitants per km²) through 11,06M in 1000AD and 15,18M in 1200AD to a pre-plague peak of 19,25M in 1347AD (12,84 per km²). Over five and a half centuries total headcount expanded by 129,4%, underpinned by heavy-plough assarting, three-field grain rotation, royal town chartering and *Ostsiedlung* colonisation. Yet expansion was sharply uneven, producing a historic north-westward shift in demographic gravity. In 800AD the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece held 28,4% of regional numbers (2,45M) and anchored Europe's largest Christian city at Constantinople (220k, peaking at 250k around 900AD). By 1347AD warfare, Fourth Crusade fragmentation and Ottoman border raids had held Greek-Bulgarian growth to 53,1%, whereas Bohemia and Moravia (+214,5%, 24,9 per km²), Hungary and Slovakia (+210,5%, 21,04 per km² despite the devastating 1241 Mongol invasion) and Piast Poland (+151,7%, 3,65M) had surged ahead. Anchored by 708 georeferenced settlements sourced strictly from institutional historical-urban and ancient-world archives (0% crowd-sourced fallback), this study establishes the pre-Black Death demographic baseline for eastern, central and south-eastern Europe.

# Background

## Geographic Corridors and Agro-Ecological Gradients

The 1.499.589,5 km² examined in this chapter form the broad eastern and south-eastern hinge of Latin and Orthodox Europe, bounded on the north by the Gulf of Finland and the Baltic shore, on the west by the Elbe-Saale, Bohemian Forest and Julian Alps, on the east by the Ruthenian forest-steppe beyond the Bug, Prut and Dniester rivers and on the south by the Aegean and Ionian seas. Unlike the compact alluvial basins of north-western Europe, this corridor traverses four distinct climatic and agricultural belts whose carrying capacities diverged markedly between 800AD and 1347AD.

At the northern edge lay the glaciated moraine plains, peatlands and mixed coniferous forests of the Baltic Lands (167.973,5 km²) and the North European Plain of Piast Poland (308.459,5 km²). Short frost-free seasons, podzolic sands and braided river floodplains kept early mediaeval farming tied to rye, oats, millet and swine herding in woodland clearings, with higher arable returns confined to loess terraces in Silesia and Lesser Poland and black-earth pockets in Kuyavia. South of the Sudetes and Ore Mountains, Bohemia and Moravia (78.306,2 km²) constituted an enclosed Hercynian basin whose loess-mantled Elbe and Morava troughs enjoyed milder summers and deep arable soils well suited to wheat, barley and brewing hops, rimmed by silver-bearing crystalline highlands that fuelled thirteenth-century upland clearance.

Across the Carpathian arc stretched the two great Danubian lowlands. Inside the mountain ring, the Kingdom of Hungary and Slovakia (140.238,2 km²) combined the fertile loess and chernozem of Transdanubia and the Great Hungarian Plain (Alföld) with the metalliferous uplands of Upper Hungary (modern Slovakia), an agro-ecological landscape whose pastoral and cereal potential had already shaped Danubian settlement for millennia [@Blanz2023Early]. Outside and astride the eastern Carpathians, Transylvania, Wallachia and Moldavia (261.865,2 km²) paired a defensible intermontane plateau with exposed Pontic steppes and Danube floodplain wetlands [@Vasile2012Considerations], where arable villages constantly competed with mounted pastoralists arriving along the Black Sea corridor.

South of the Sava and the Lower Danube, topography fractured into karst plateaux, narrow tectonic basins and Mediterranean peninsulas. Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia (126.176,8 km²) straddled the Alpine-Pannonian saddle and the Dinaric karst, separating wet Slavonian river valleys from limestone pasture and maritime Dalmatian harbours. Farther south-east, Mediaeval Serbia, Montenegro and Albania (155.482,7 km²) grouped the Morava-Vardar transit corridor, the fertile Kosovo and Metohija basins and high summer pastures where upland dairying and transhumant flocks remained essential complements to valley cereal cropping [@Stojanovski2020Living]. Finally, the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece (266.186,1 km²) combined the broad Danubian grain plain of Moesia and the Maritsa valley of Thrace with the fragmented coastal plains, olive groves and island archipelagos of the Aegean — the only zone in the entire chapter that preserved direct late antique urban institutions and maritime commercial networks into the ninth century.

## State Formation, Frontier Colonisation and Steppe Incursions

In 800AD political geography across this vast expanse was starkly asymmetric. South of the Balkan range, the Byzantine Empire was emerging from its seventh- and eighth-century demographic nadir, defending imperial Thrace, Thessalonica and coastal Greece against the expanding First Bulgarian Empire anchored in north-eastern Bulgaria. North of the Danube, however, literacy, coined currency and permanent taxation scarcely existed. Charlemagne's destruction of the Avar Khaganate in 791-796 cleared the Middle Danube for Slavonic principalities — chief among them Great Moravia in the ninth century — while west of the Vistula tribal Polabian, Lechitic and Czech communities clustered around timber-and-earth ringworks (*grody*) guarding river crossings and forest clearings [@Tomasek2018Sclavos; @Skrzynska2025Grodowa].

Between 895 and 1000AD three decisive political consolidations redrew the demographic map of East-Central Europe. First, the Magyar arrival in the Carpathian Basin (895-896) shattered Great Moravia, shifted nomadic horsemen into the Hungarian plain and temporarily destabilised Moravian and Pannonian farmsteads before the conversion and coronation of Stephen I in 1000AD anchored a sedentary Christian monarchy. Second, the Premyslid dukes of Prague unified Bohemia and annexed Moravia, tying the upper Elbe basin to imperial German trade and ecclesiastical organisation. Third, the Piast dynasty forged a territorial state linking Greater Poland (Gniezno and Poznan), Lesser Poland (Krakow), Silesia and Pomerania, accepting Latin Christianity under Mieszko I in 966 and establishing a royal fisc backed by ducal strongholds and service villages [@Skrzynska2025Grodowa].

From 1100AD to 1347AD internal agrarian reform and western migration accelerated population growth across the Latin north-west far faster than anywhere in the Orthodox south-east. Heavy iron mouldboard ploughs, horse collars, watermills and regular three-field rotations spread eastward alongside the legal revolution of *ius Teutonicum* (German town and village law). Polish dukes, Premyslid kings and Hungarian monarchs actively recruited German, Flemish and Walloon *hospites* (chartered colonists) to clear forest uplands in Silesia, northern Bohemia, the Carpathian foothills of Slovakia and southern Transylvania, founding hundreds of planned market towns and nucleated linear villages (*Waldhufendörfer*). In the north-east, conquest replaced invitation: after 1200AD the Livonian Swordbrothers and the Teutonic Order subdued Livonia, Estonia and Old Prussia, planting Hanseatic ports at Riga, Reval and Elbing while provoking the political unification of the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania along the Nemunas and Neris valleys.

Steppe mobility remained the chief counter-weight to sedentary growth. Pechenegs and Cumans repeatedly raided Bulgaria, Thrace, Wallachia and eastern Hungary during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Then, in the spring of 1241, Batu Khan's Mongol armies crushed Polish-Silesian forces at Legnica and annihilated Bela IV's Hungarian host at the River Sajo (Mohi), ravaging the Great Plain, Transylvania and eastern Poland before withdrawing to the lower Volga in 1242. Recovery from 1242 to 1347 was rapid in Hungary and Poland — aided by royal stone-castle construction, fresh Cuman and German settlement and an explosion of Central European silver and gold mining at Kutna Hora, Jihlava, Kremnica and Novo Brdo — but in Wallachia and Moldavia Golden Horde suzerainty delayed consolidated princely states until the early fourteenth century.

## Urban Continua and the Byzantine-Latin Commercial Fault Line

Urbanisation across these eight sub-regions followed two wholly separate chronologies [@Bairoch1988; @Buringh2021]. Along the Bosporus, the Aegean and the Adriatic, mediaeval towns stood directly on classical foundations. Constantinople remained a demographic colossus without peer in Christendom from 800AD to 1204AD, provisioned by Thracian grain, Black Sea fish and Aegean oil, while Thessalonica, Adrianople, Philippopolis (Plovdiv), Dyrrhachium (Durres), Athens and the Dalmatian communes maintained walled episcopal seats and craft guilds throughout the early Middle Ages.

North of the Danube, urban life was a mediaeval creation. Ninth- and tenth-century Baltic and Slavic emporia such as Wolin at the Oder mouth, Mikulcice in Moravia and early Gniezno functioned as timber trading stations or ducal fortress-suburbs (*podgrodzia*) rather than chartered municipalities. Only after 1150-1200AD did a durable network of stone-walled merchant cities crystallise around Prague, Wroclaw, Krakow, Gdansk, Buda, Esztergom, Olomouc, Brno, Brasov, Cluj and Riga. By 1347AD the balance had tilted decisively: Constantinople had fallen to 90k after the Latin sack of 1204 and Palaiologan civil wars, whereas scores of mid-sized chartered towns across Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, Transylvania and Serbia had multiplied regional commercial density and tied the eastern European interior directly to Hanseatic, German and Venetian markets [@Malanima1998; @Buringh2021].

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Areal Calibration and Fiscal-Archaeological Triangulation

Reconstructing population across 1.499.589,5 km² between 800AD and 1347AD cannot rely on universal censuses, because no state in the domain enumerated all inhabitants before the early modern era. Instead, MAGNETIC calibrates sub-regional headcounts at four canonical benchmarks — 800AD, 1000AD, 1200AD and 1347AD — by combining four independent lines of demographic evidence within fixed equal-area polygons derived from the chapter's areal mask.

First, surviving mediaeval fiscal and ecclesiastical registers anchor terminal 1300-1347AD levels where they exist. For Piast Poland, fourteenth-century papal Peter's Pence (*denarius sancti Petri*) hearth assessments from the 1320s-1340s — combined with later village court and parish reconstructions — constrain the population of Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, Silesia and Mazovia to roughly 10-13 inhabitants per km² across the broader Polish landmass [@Guzowski2013; @Russell1958]. For Hungary, the papal tithe lists of 1332-1337 provide parish counts across Transdanubia, Upper Hungary and Transylvania, enabling reconstruction of post-Mongol recovery densities. In the Byzantine Balkans, monastic *praktika* (household tax inventories from Macedonia, Chalkidiki and western Thrace) document peasant *staseis* (hearth holdings), family sizes averaging 4,2 to 4,8 persons and village demographic turnover through the early fourteenth century, while Nemanjic Serbian monastic *chrysobulls* (Decani, Sveti Stefan, Arhandjeli) enumerate thousands of individual arable and pastoral households across Kosovo, Metohija and southern Serbia.

Second, archaeological settlement grids, stronghold distributions and funerary series bridge the pre-documentary centuries from 800AD to 1200AD. Early mediaeval stronghold networks in Poland and Polabia [@Skrzynska2025Grodowa; @Tomasek2018Sclavos], biritual Lower Danube cemeteries between Bulgaria and Wallachia [@Staykov2022Necropolises], bioarchaeological series from the Prut-Dniester corridor [@Simalcsik2018Cases] and isotopic mobility studies along the Alpine-Danubian fringe [@Velte2023Raetia] establish relative village multiplication rates and frontier settlement density before royal charters begin.

Third, high-resolution palynological records across Poland, Bohemia, Greece and the Balkans independently test cereal expansion versus woodland regeneration [@Izdebski2022]. Pollen cores confirm steady arable expansion across East-Central Europe from 900AD through 1347AD — matching the demographic climb in Poland, Bohemia and Hungary — while capturing localised fourteenth-century agrarian stagnation in parts of Greece and Thrace even prior to the Black Death [@Izdebski2022; @Campbell2016].

Fourth, pre-industrial demographic ceilings and compound annual growth bounds guard against chronicler exaggeration. Sustained long-run growth over two centuries in mediaeval agrarian economies rarely exceeded 0,2-0,25% per annum even during active frontier colonisation, while national-scale pre-plague densities in fertile Central European loess basins plateaued around 20-25 inhabitants per km² — substantially below the 35-45 per km² of northern Italy or Flanders, yet well above the 5-8 per km² of boreal Baltic or steppe-exposed Moldavian marches [@Broadberry2015; @Malanima1998; @Campbell2016].

## Settlement Gazetteer Architecture and Provenance Harmonisation

To anchor macro-regional curves in explicit spatial coordinates, MAGNETIC assembles a geocoded settlement register of 708 active localities across 22 modern jurisdictions spanning the 800-1347AD domain. Candidate localities passed through a four-wave saturation protocol auditing institutional urban datasets and ancient-world continuity gazetteers before excluding 85 out-of-domain or duplicate records. Exactly zero crowd-sourced entries were admitted (0% crowd share). Table 1 summarises the provenance composition of the register.

Two complementary archival streams shape the spatial structure of the register. Wave 1 ingested 230 urban centres (35,27%) from Eltjo Buringh's longitudinal European city series [@Buringh2021], providing century-by-century urban estimates from 800AD to 1300AD plus interpolated pre-Black Death 1347AD values across every one of the eight sub-regions. Wave 2 added 362 classical-to-mediaeval continuity localities (64,73%) from the Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer, assigned standardised continuity population tiers (510 for minor walled villages and rural loci, 1,5k for fortified regional towns and 3,6k for major classical-mediaeval nuclei). Waves 3 and 4 audited municipal backfills and sub-regional gaps without requiring supplementary additions.

# Validation

## Cross-Checking Against Archival Tax Rolls, Chronicles and Comparative Series

Independent benchmarking against published historical-demographic literature confirms that MAGNETIC's sub-regional curves sit squarely within the consensus envelope while correcting older twentieth-century undercounts of East-Central Europe. Josiah Cox Russell's pioneer compilation estimated combined Poland, Bohemia, Hungary and the Balkans at roughly 12-15M around 1300-1340AD [@Russell1958], a figure now widely recognised by Central European medievalists as too low for Bohemia and Poland because it underweighted thirteenth-century upland clearance and underestimated household multipliers in Peter's Pence assessments [@Guzowski2013]. Raising Bohemia and Moravia to 1,95M (24,9 per km²) and Piast Poland (within its 308.459,5 km² polygon) to 3,65M (11,83 per km²) aligns MAGNETIC closely with modern Polish and Czech parish reconstructions and with high-resolution pollen records demonstrating sustained forest clearance across Silesia, Greater Poland and Bohemia right up to 1347AD [@Izdebski2022; @Guzowski2013].

At the western comparative edge, Bohemia's 1347AD density of 24,9 inhabitants per km² and Hungary-Slovakia's 21,04 per km² are structurally coherent against England (roughly 4,75M on 130.000 km², or 36,5 per km² on the eve of the Black Death) and northern-central Italy (40-45 per km²) [@Broadberry2015; @Malanima1998; @Campbell2016]. Because East-Central Europe experienced its heavy-plough and town-chartering boom one to two centuries later than England, France or Lombardy, its frontier kingdoms reached two-thirds of English density in the Bohemian core and roughly one-third in lowland Poland, while retaining ample uncultivated land buffers that cushioned them against the severe 1315-1317 Great Famine that struck north-western Europe [@Campbell2016].

Urban benchmarks likewise pass cross-checking against Bairoch et al. and Buringh [@Bairoch1988; @Buringh2021]. In 1347AD the 291 Buringh cities active across the chapter total 879k urban residents (a recorded urban ratio of 4,55% across the 19,33M aggregate, down slightly from 923k at 1300AD owing to late Byzantine contraction in Constantinople, Thessalonica and Bulgaria). That ratio matches expectations for a predominantly agrarian corridor whose urban share trailed Italy (around 21%) and Flanders (around 25%) yet rose sharply above its ninth-century baseline outside the Bosporus [@Malanima1998; @Bairoch1988].

## Implied Growth Rates, Carrying-Capacity Ceilings and Spatial Plausibility

Checking implied compound annual growth rates (CAGR) across every sub-regional interval verifies demographic plausibility under pre-industrial mortality regimes, where life expectancy at birth hovered around 24-30 years and periodic harvest failures, steppe raids and regional epidemics checked explosive natural increase [@Benedictow2004; @Campbell2016]. Table 2 details interval growth rates and cumulative expansion multipliers for all eight sub-regions from 800AD to 1347AD.

Every interval sits within biological and historical realism. Domain-wide annual growth averaged 0,14% between 800AD and 1000AD, rose to 0,15% between 1000AD and 1200AD and held steady at 0,15% between 1200AD and 1347AD. The steepest sustained climb occurred in Bohemia and Moravia between 1200AD and 1347AD (0,25% per annum), reflecting combined natural increase and documented Saxon-Franconian immigration into upland farming and silver-mining towns. Conversely, the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans decelerated from 0,09% per annum during the Macedonian agrarian revival (800-1000AD) to 0,06% between 1200AD and 1347AD, cleanly mirroring the political disintegration of Byzantium after 1204 and chronic fourteenth-century warfare across Thrace and Macedonia [@Totomanova2017Synodikon; @Campbell2016].

# Results

## Macro-Regional Trajectory and the North-Westward Shift of Demographic Weight

Across the 547 years preceding the Black Death, total population in East-Central Europe, the Baltic and the Balkans more than doubled, climbing from 8,64M in 800AD to 11,35M in 1000AD (+31,4%), 15,43M in 1200AD (+35,9%) and 19,33M in 1347AD (+25,3%). Mean regional density rose correspondingly from 5,74 to 12,85 inhabitants per km². Figure 1 plots the aggregate climb alongside leading sub-regional curves and terminal 1347AD densities, while Table 3 reports the full benchmark matrix across all eight sub-regions.

The defining structural feature of Table 3 is the reallocation of demographic weight from the south-eastern Mediterranean-Balkan rim toward the Central European interior. In 800AD the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece (2,45M) alone equalled 81,1% of the three Latin core kingdoms combined — Bohemia and Moravia (620k), Hungary and Slovakia (950k) and Piast Poland (1,45M, totalling 3,02M) — while enjoying a mean density (9,2 per km²) nearly double Poland's (4,7 per km²). Over the next five centuries that balance inverted. By 1347AD Poland, Bohemia-Moravia and Hungary-Slovakia collectively reached 8,55M (44,2% of the entire domain, up from 35% in 800AD), while the Byzantine-Bulgarian share shrank from 28,4% to 19,4%. The Danubian and Slavic woodland frontier had become a major demographic centre in its own right.

## Piast Poland and the Mechanics of Ostsiedlung

Within its 308.459,5 km² polygon spanning Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, Silesia, Pomerania and Mazovia, the Piast Kingdom of Poland rose from 1,45M inhabitants in 800AD (4,7 per km²) to 1,95M in 1000AD (6,32 per km²), 2,85M in 1200AD (9,24 per km²) and 3,65M in 1347AD (11,83 per km²). Overall growth of 151,7% added 2,2M people, making Poland the single largest contributor to aggregate regional expansion after 1000AD.

During the ninth and tenth centuries Polish settlement concentrated along the Warta, Noteć, middle Oder and upper Vistula valleys, anchored by earth-and-timber ducal strongholds (*grody*) whose dense local networks have been documented archaeologically across Greater Poland and Mazovia [@Skrzynska2025Grodowa]. Along the western frontier, Polabian and Pomeranian Slavic tribes maintained dispersed agrarian districts and maritime trading hubs [@Tomasek2018Sclavos]; Wolin at the Oder estuary reached an early mediaeval zenith of 9k around 1000AD before Danish raids and silting shifted Baltic commerce eastward to Szczecin and Gdansk.

After 1138AD, Poland's territorial fragmentation into rival Piast duchies paradoxically accelerated demographic growth. Competing dukes in Silesia, Greater Poland, Lesser Poland and Mazovia sought cash rents and military dues by granting immunised charters (*locatio*) under Magdeburg and Sroda law. German, Flemish and Walloon peasants cleared dense forests along the Sudeten foothills, the Oder floodplain and eastern Pomerania, while native Polish villages were reorganised on regular three-field hides (*lany*) paying fixed grain and silver rents rather than archaic labour tributes [@Guzowski2013]. Even the devastating 1241 Mongol incursion through Sandomierz, Krakow and Legnica — and follow-up raids in 1259 and 1287 — caused only transient regional setbacks in Lesser Poland and Silesia. By 1347AD, under Casimir III the Great, a reunified crown rested on a prosperous rural economy whose pollen profiles show steady cereal expansion and minimal late-mediaeval abandonment [@Izdebski2022], crowned by growing commercial towns at Gdansk (13,1k), Wroclaw (11k, peaking at 12k in 1300), Krakow (10k), Goerlitz (6,2k) and Szczecin (5k).

## Premyslid Bohemia, Moravia and the Central European Silver Boom

Bohemia and Moravia (78.306,2 km²) recorded the most rapid proportional growth (+214,5%) and the highest pre-plague density (24,9 per km²) of any sub-region in this chapter. Headcount climbed from 620k in 800AD (7,92 per km²) to 880k in 1000AD (11,24 per km²), 1,35M in 1200AD (17,24 per km²) and 1,95M in 1347AD.

In the ninth century the demographic centre lay in southern Moravia along the lower Morava and Dyje rivers, where Great Moravian fortified agglomerations at Mikulcice, Pohansko and Stare Mesto flourished on fertile loess terraces until Magyar raids broke the Moravian state around 906AD. Thereafter gravity shifted westward into the sheltered Bohemian basin under the Premyslid dynasty. Prague, a modest 1k hillfort cluster in 800AD, jumped to 10k by 1000AD as a transcontinental slave, fur and silver mart described by Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, before nearly doubling to 19,2k by 1347AD as Charles IV prepared to elevate it into an imperial capital and university city.

The decisive demographic surge occurred between 1200AD and 1347AD (+44,4%, or 0,25% per annum). Royal and monastic lords opened the forested mountain ring of the Ore Mountains, Sudetes and Bohemian-Moravian Highlands to colonist villages while rich silver lodes discovered at Jihlava (1240s) and Kutna Hora (1290s) drew thousands of Saxon, Bavarian and Franconian miners and merchants. Kutna Hora swelled from 2k in 1000AD to 8,5k in 1347AD, underwriting the Prague *groschen* minted from 1300AD — the hard silver currency of late mediaeval East-Central Europe — while regional centres at Plzen (9k peak in 1300, 7,4k in 1347), Olomouc (8k peak), Brno (7k peak) and Jihlava (6k peak) knitted Bohemia and Moravia into an integrated urban-rural market whose archival and courtly continuity extended deep into the Renaissance [@Manas2021Johann; @Velte2023Raetia].

## Arpad Hungary, the 1241 Mongol Shock and Angevin Recovery

The Kingdom of Hungary and Slovakia (140.238,2 km²) achieved the second steepest expansion (+210,5%) and second highest terminal density (21,04 per km²), rising from 950k in 800AD (6,77 per km²) to 1,45M in 1000AD (10,34 per km²), 2,25M in 1200AD (16,04 per km²) and 2,95M in 1347AD.

Following the collapse of the Avar Khaganate in the 790s, the Carpathian Basin held a sparse mixed population of Slavs, surviving Avars and Frankish-border colonists until the Magyar confederation entered through the Veraetske Pass in 895-896. Modern archaeology and palaeo-dietary research on the Hungarian lowlands emphasise how rapidly the newcomers integrated into an ancient mixed-pastoral and cereal landscape [@Blanz2023Early]. After Otto I's victory at the Lechfeld (955) ended western raids, Grand Prince Geza and King Stephen I (crowned 1000AD) organised royal counties (*comitatus*), bishoprics and Latin Benedictine abbeys. During the eleventh and twelfth centuries western *hospites* settled wine-producing hills, northern Slovakian river valleys (Spis and Gemer) and early royal towns at Esztergom (6k in 1000AD), Szekesfehervar (4k in 1200AD) and Pest-Buda (9k combined by 1200AD).

No demographic shock in mediaeval East-Central Europe before 1347 rivalled the Mongol invasion of 1241-1242. Following the destruction of the royal army at Mohi in April 1241, Mongol columns systematically depopulated the open villages of the Alföld between the Danube and the Tisza and burned unfortified lowland towns such as Pest and Oradea. Historians debate exact mortality — contemporary estimates ranging from 15% to 25% of the entire kingdom's population, reaching 40-50% in exposed Great Plain counties — yet the 1200-1347AD benchmark interval still posts net growth of +31,1% (+700k) because post-1242 recovery was extraordinarily vigorous. King Bela IV shifted the royal centre to the fortified hilltop of Buda (6,9k by 1347, paired with 5,9k across the Danube at Pest), licensed scores of stone castles, invited tens of thousands of Cumans and Jasz horsemen to repopulate the empty steppe plains and expanded German mining towns in Upper Hungary. Under Angevin rulers Charles Robert and Louis I, gold from Kremnica and silver from Banska Stiavnica turned Bratislava (4,5k in 1347) and Kosice (5k) into thriving commercial nodes, carrying the kingdom past 2,95M on the eve of the plague.

## Transylvania, Wallachia and Moldavia Between Crown and Steppe

Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania (261.865,2 km²) expanded more moderately (+114,3%), advancing from 1,05M in 800AD (4,01 per km²) to 1,35M in 1000AD (5,16 per km²), 1,75M in 1200AD (6,68 per km²) and 2,25M in 1347AD (8,59 per km²). That modest mean density conceals a sharp geographical divide along the Carpathian crest.

Inside the mountain ring, Transylvania followed the Central European trajectory. Absorbed progressively into the Hungarian crown during the eleventh and twelfth centuries, it received Magyar noble estates, Szekely border communities along the eastern passes and German-speaking Transylvanian Saxons summoned under Geza II (1141-1162) and confirmed by the *Diploma Andreanum* of 1224. Saxon colonists cleared valleys and built stone-walled trading cities — Brasov climbing from 1k in 1100AD to 7,2k in 1347AD, Cluj reaching 7k by 1300AD (6k in 1347AD) alongside Sibiu and Bistrita — pushing Transylvanian densities toward 12-15 per km².

Outside the Carpathians, Wallachia and Moldavia lay directly astride the western terminus of the Eurasian steppe. Early mediaeval settlements along the Lower Danube and the Prut-Dniester corridor shared cultural and funerary traditions with First Bulgarian communities [@Staykov2022Necropolises] while bearing direct bioarchaeological markers of steppe contact [@Simalcsik2018Cases]. Pecheneg, Uze, Cuman and (after 1241) Golden Horde dominance discouraged permanent open-plain villages across the Baragan and Budjak steppes, concentrating Romanian-speaking (*Vlach*) peasants and pastoralists in wooded Sub-Carpathian hills, river valleys and the wetland fringes of the Danube Delta [@Vasile2012Considerations]. As Mongol power receded after 1300AD, princely consolidation under Basarab I in Wallachia (securing independence at Posada in 1330) and the early Moldavian voivodes stimulated rapid lowland recolonisation, monastic manuscript transmission from Bulgaria [@Cholova2012Spreading], early regional coinage [@Olariu1999Study] and the growth of court and transit centres at Tirgoviste (14,5k in 1347AD) and Suceava (13k peak in 1300AD, 10,9k in 1347AD).

## The Baltic Frontier: Crusader Towns and Grand Ducal Lithuania

The Baltic Lands (167.973,5 km², covering modern Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania) grew by 133,3% over the domain, moving from 420k in 800AD (2,5 per km²) through 560k in 1000AD (3,33 per km²) and 780k in 1200AD (4,64 per km²) to 980k in 1347AD (5,83 per km²). Despite more than doubling, the eastern Baltic remained the sparsest sub-region in this chapter — a direct consequence of short northern growing seasons, extensive bogs and vulnerability to cooler climatic spells comparable to Europe's boreal Atlantic margin [@Dugmore2012; @Campbell2016].

Prior to 1200AD settlement was overwhelmingly rural and polycentric, organised around timber hillforts (*piliskalni*) and parish districts inhabited by Finnic Estonians and Livs in the north and Baltic Latgallians, Semigallians, Curonians and Lithuanians in the south. Viking-age silver hoards attest to vigorous riverine fur, wax and amber exchange along the Daugava and Nemunas, yet no permanent stone cities existed. After 1200AD the Northern Crusades fractured the region along two contrasting demographic paths. In Livonia and Estonia, German crusaders, Danish kings and Hanseatic merchants established coastal and riverine walled ports — Riga soaring from a 2k foundation in 1200AD to 7k by 1300-1347AD, Tallinn rising to 2,4k and Tartu reaching 2k — while decades of siege warfare and peasant uprisings (culminating in the St George's Night Uprising of 1343-1345) periodically thinned rural districts. South of the Daugava, by contrast, Baltic resistance forged the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Mindaugas, Vytenis and Gediminas. Although Teutonic border raids (*Reisen*) created a depopulated wilderness belt (*Wildnis*) along the Prussian and Samogitian frontier, interior Lithuania expanded steadily around Vilnius (4,5k in 1347AD) and Trakai, absorbing densely settled Ruthenian principalities to the east and building a demographic reserve strong enough to contest Teutonic supremacy for a century.

## The Dinaric-Adriatic Corridor and Nemanjic Serbia

The western and central Balkans divide analytically into two sub-regions of similar pre-plague density: Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia (126.176,8 km², rising from 720k in 800AD to 1,65M in 1347AD, 13,08 per km², +129,2%) and Mediaeval Serbia, Montenegro and Albania (155.482,7 km², rising from 980k to 2,15M, 13,83 per km², +119,4%).

In Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia, population clustered along two poles separated by barren karst. To the north-west, Alpine Carniola, Styria and the fertile Sava-Drava valleys of Slavonia integrated into Bavarian-Habsburg and Hungarian feudal lordship, benefiting from German upland colonisation and Alpine-Danubian commercial corridors [@Velte2023Raetia], with Ljubljana rising from 2k in 800AD to 4k in 1300AD (3,5k in 1347AD). Along the Adriatic shore, Roman-descended communes from Trieste (5k peak in 1300AD) and Koper (3k) through Rovinj (3k) to Zadar, Split and Dubrovnik prospered under Venetian or Hungarian-Croatian commercial ties [@Malanima1998]. Between them, the Bosnian Banate grew steadily from the twelfth century as rural clearance in the Bosna and Vrbas valleys combined with silver and lead mining during the fourteenth century (the Sarajevo precursor reaching 2,4k-3k).

Farther south-east, Mediaeval Serbia, Montenegro and Albania experienced its strongest agrarian and urban surge between 1180AD and 1347AD under the Nemanjic dynasty. Upland transhumant pastoralism — a deep-rooted Balkan subsistence adaptation [@Stojanovski2020Living] — meshed with expanding valley wheat and viticulture across Rashka, Zeta, Kosovo and northern Macedonia. Royal charters granted to great monasteries such as Studenica, Banjska and Visoki Decani register densely packed peasant villages alongside specialised Saxon (*Sasi*) mining towns opened at Brskovo, Rudnik, Trepca and Novo Brdo after 1250AD. Strategic transit hubs expanded in step: Belgrade at the Sava-Danube confluence climbed from 3k in 800AD to 14k in 1200AD and 24,2k in 1347AD, Prizren reached 10k in 1300AD (8,5k in 1347AD), Nis rose to 8,4k in 1347AD, while Adriatic and Via Egnatia gateways at Durres (6k peak), Ohrid (5k) and Bitola (5k) anchored trade between the Aegean and Italy. By 1346AD Emperor Stefan Dusan ruled a Balkan realm near its mediaeval demographic zenith, just one year before plague reached the Adriatic coast [@Benedictow2004].

## The Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece: Early Primacy and Late Stagnation

The Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece (266.186,1 km²) started 800AD as the demographic giant of the entire region (2,45M, 9,2 per km²) and ended 1347AD still marginally the most populous single sub-region (3,75M, 14,09 per km²), yet its cumulative growth of 53,1% lagged far behind every northern neighbour.

Between 800AD and 1200AD the region enjoyed a genuine, if contested, mediaeval renaissance. After repelling early Arab sieges and absorbing Slavic rural settlements across Thrace, Macedonia and mainland Greece, Byzantium under the Macedonian and Komnenian dynasties expanded arable acreage, monetised provincial taxes and revived provincial textile and silk cities at Thessalonica (40k-50k), Thebes, Corinth and Athens (9k in 800AD rising to 21k in 1200AD). Across the Balkan mountains, the First Bulgarian Empire achieved remarkable ninth- and tenth-century vitality: Khan Boris's conversion and Tsar Symeon I's imperial ambitions raised Preslav from 4k in 800AD to a peak of 35k around 900AD before Rus' and Byzantine armies sacked the city in 971AD, reducing it to 10k by 1000AD and 1k by 1300AD. Following Basil II's reconquest (1018), Bulgarian demography recovered under the Second Bulgarian Empire (founded 1185), documented in ecclesiastical and royal memorials such as the Synodikon of Orthodoxy [@Totomanova2017Synodikon], lifting its capital Veliko Turnovo from 3k in 1000AD to 13k in 1300AD alongside Plovdiv (13k), Sliven (11k) and Shumen (8k).

The turning point was 1204AD. The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople shattered imperial unity into warring Latin, Venetian, Epirote, Nicaean and Bulgarian polities. Constantinople's population, already easing from 250k in 900AD to 150k in 1200AD, dropped to 100k by 1300AD and 90k by 1347AD. Although Athens (29,3k), Thessalonica (46,1k in 1347AD) and Venetian-ruled Crete (Iraklion peaking at 7k) sustained commercial vitality, destructive fourteenth-century shocks — Catalan Company depredations in Thrace and Thessaly, Serbian conquests in Macedonia, the devastating Byzantine civil wars of 1341-1347 and early Turkish raids across the Dardanelles — emptied Thracian and eastern Macedonian villages [@Izdebski2022; @Campbell2016]. When Genoese galleys from Caffa carried plague into Constantinople and Thessalonica in the summer and autumn of 1347 [@Benedictow2004], they struck a Greek-Thracian landscape already exhausted by half a century of warfare.

The rank-size distribution in Figure 2 exhibits a tight power-law fit ($\alpha = 0,7$, $R^2 = 0,96$) across the urban and town tiers, accompanied by one massive primate outlier at rank 1: Constantinople (250k peak in 900AD), sitting more than three times above the regression line and five times above second-ranked Thessalonica (50k). That sub-Zipfian slope ($\alpha = 0,7 < 1$) reflects the geopolitical reality of the domain: rather than forming a single integrated urban system, East-Central Europe, the Baltic and the Balkans comprised half a dozen separate royal and imperial hierarchies — Byzantine, Bulgarian, Serbian, Hungarian, Bohemian, Polish and Hanseatic-Livonian — each supporting its own cluster of 8k-25k capitals and regional ports [@Bairoch1988; @Buringh2021]. Equally striking in Table 4 is urban churn between 800AD and 1347AD. Early Byzantine and First Bulgarian capitals (Constantinople and Preslav) contracted sharply from their ninth- and tenth-century peaks, whereas Central European and Danubian towns (Prague, Belgrade, Tirgoviste, Gdansk, Wroclaw, Krakow, Suceava and Prizren) accounted for virtually all net urban growth after 1100AD.

# Limitations

Four structural limitations qualify these estimates and must be borne in mind when comparing sub-regions or linking Chapter 10 to later early modern series.

First, sub-regional totals between 800AD and 1200AD remain interpolations anchored to archaeological settlement density, stronghold grids and agro-ecological carrying capacity rather than direct headcounts. True uncertainty intervals widen backward in time — roughly plus or minus 12-15% at 1347AD where papal tithes, Peter's Pence and Byzantine *praktika* exist, widening to plus or minus 25-30% at 800AD across the non-literate Slavic, Baltic and extra-Carpathian steppe zones [@Russell1958; @Guzowski2013].

Second, benchmark spacing at 200-year and 147-year intervals (800, 1000, 1200 and 1347AD) necessarily smooths acute mid-interval shocks. Most notably, the catastrophic Mongol devastation of Hungary, Transylvania and southern Poland in 1241-1242 sits inside the 1200-1347AD window; although Hungary's lower growth rate in 1200-1347AD (0,18% per annum) relative to 1000-1200AD (0,22% per annum) captures the net demographic drag of the invasion, the four-point curve cannot render the sharp V-shaped trough of 1242-1260 directly. The same applies to the Great Moravian collapse around 906AD and the Latin conquest of Constantinople in 1204AD.

Third, spatial recording density in the 825-site gazetteer is strongly skewed by classical archival survival. Because the Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer documents classical-to-mediaeval Greek and Aegean continuity sites exhaustively, the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece hold 432 localities (52,36% of the chapter gazetteer, including 363 in modern Greece alone), whereas the Baltic Lands hold only 14 recorded urban entries (1,7%, all from Buringh). Macro-regional headcounts therefore rely on agro-ecological density calibration and archival tax benchmarks rather than raw gazetteer counts.

Fourth, fixed modern-aligned equal-area polygons inevitably trim or overlap fluid mediaeval borders. Trieste falls along the Adriatic edge of the Slovenia-Croatia-Bosnia mask; Goerlitz sits on the western edge of Piast Silesia; Vidin and Silistra enter the Danube margin of the Wallachia-Moldavia-Transylvania polygon. These minor boundary overlaps are preserved transparently so that total regional land area (1.504.688,1 km²) reconciles cleanly across chronological chapters without double-counting European landmass.

# Conclusion

Between 800AD and 1347AD East-Central Europe, the Baltic lands and the Balkans moved from a sparsely settled frontier dominated by Constantinople to a densely farmed, monetised and increasingly urbanised macro-region of 19,33M inhabitants. Aggregate population expanded by 123,7%, raising mean density from 5,74 to 12,85 inhabitants per km² across 1.504.688,1 km². That growth was powered less by the ancient Mediterranean core than by the agrarian, legal and mining revolution north of the Danube: Bohemia and Moravia tripled to 1,95M (24,9 per km²) and Hungary and Slovakia tripled to 2,95M (21,04 per km²) despite surviving the Mongol catastrophe of 1241, while Piast Poland reached 3,65M (11,83 per km²) through *Ostsiedlung* and internal clearance. Meanwhile, the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans grew only 53,1% to 3,75M, losing its ninth-century primacy as Constantinople contracted from 250k to 90k. When the Black Death crossed the Bosporus and Adriatic in 1347AD [@Benedictow2004; @Izdebski2022], it encountered a region whose demographic centre of gravity had permanently shifted north-westward into the Polish, Bohemian, Hungarian and Serbian heartlands.

Two diagnostic patterns stand out in Table 5. First, recorded 1347AD urban shares from the Buringh corpus peak in the Byzantine-Bulgarian Balkans and Greece (7,95%, anchored by Constantinople, Thessalonica and Athens), followed by Mediaeval Serbia, Montenegro and Albania (4,6%, led by Belgrade, Prizren and Nis) and Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania (4,16%, led by Tirgoviste, Suceava, Brasov and Cluj). Second, Piast Poland (4%), Bohemia and Moravia (3,88%) and Hungary and Slovakia (3,76%) cluster tightly in the 3,8-4% bracket — a realistic reflection of frontier kingdoms whose dense networks of chartered small market towns (500-2.000 inhabitants) lay largely below the threshold of Buringh's pan-European urban register, while the Baltic Lands (2,53%) and Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia (1,88%) remained overwhelmingly rural outside their coastal Hanseatic and Adriatic ports. Detailed site-by-site provenance and jurisdictional breakdowns appear in the companion settlements gazetteer.
